None mentions the European Accessibility Act, which applies to e-commerce services sold to EU consumers from 28 June 2025.

Site search tested with query types: every page says 'make search visible'. None gives a repeatable test sheet (misspelling, synonym, product attribute, SKU or model number, non-product query such as 'returns') or tells the auditor to pull zero-result queries from the site search log first.

Performance with numbers: only Design Monks mentions Core Web Vitals, without thresholds. No page gives the 'good' thresholds (LCP 2.5 s, INP 200 ms, CLS 0.1 at the 75th percentile, web.dev) or ties INP to store interactions (filter taps, variant swatches, add to cart).

Pre-audit data: Baymard sets up the evaluation environment but not analytics. No page lists the store data to pull before the review: GA4 funnel exploration split by device (open funnel, so returning shoppers who start at checkout count), site search log, return reasons, support ticket tags, Core Web Vitals field data.

outline.h2: What does an e-commerce UX audit check that a general UX audit skips?
outline.answerHint: An e-commerce UX audit follows a shopper's path through the store, from site search and category filters to the product detail page, cart and guest checkout, and scores each step against e-commerce usability research. A general UX audit scores flows against Nielsen's 10 heuristics without store-specific rules such as total cost before payment.
points: Intro (60-second phone test, see variety). Before the first H2: ask the reader to do three things on their own store, on their phone, on mobile data: search for a product with one letter wrong, add a product with a size or colour to the cart, and reach the payment step as a guest. Each failure points to one audit area covered below. The keyword goes in the first sentence (carrier above). Then 2 sentences on what the post gives: a checklist by funnel step, a scoring method and what to send for a quote.
Link UP to the hub early with the anchor 'e-commerce UX design services' (within the first 300 words).

Bold answer, then 3–4 sentences: heuristic evaluation is the method; store rules come from Baymard Institute research (cite its public cart abandonment page: 70.22% average across 50 studies, fact-checker to confirm). Do not describe Baymard's paid guideline database or copy its audit areas.
Visual 1: store funnel audit map (see visuals). The text version sits under it.

One sentence that the general UX audit method (heuristics, analytics, session recordings, accessibility check) is described on the UX audit hub; this is the ONE cross-hub link in the post: /services/ux-audit-services/#what-does-a-ux-audit-include.

outline.h2: Which store data should you pull before the audit starts?
outline.answerHint: Pull four data sets before anyone opens the store: a GA4 funnel exploration split by device, the site search log with zero-result queries, return and support-ticket reasons, and Core Web Vitals field data from PageSpeed Insights. They show where the audit should look first.
points: Numbered steps (ol). GA4: build a funnel exploration (view_item_list -> view_item -> add_to_cart -> begin_checkout -> add_shipping_info -> add_payment_info -> purchase, the GA4 recommended e-commerce events), make it open so shoppers who start at checkout in a later session count, and break it down by device category. Cite the GA4 Help Center article. Fact-checker: confirm the event names against Google's recommended events list.

Session recordings and heatmaps: Hotjar or Microsoft Clarity, filtered to sessions that dropped at the worst step (rage clicks, dead clicks, form field hesitation). The hub uses Hotjar; Microsoft Clarity is a free alternative.
Site search log: the top queries and the zero-result queries (from the platform's search report or the search vendor).
Return reasons and support tickets: 'wrong size' and 'not as pictured' point at the product detail page, not the warehouse.
Visual 2: pre-audit data pull card (see visuals).

Lead moment 1: stores often discover here that their funnel events are missing or duplicated. One natural sentence: we check the tracking in the first days of the audit before trusting any drop-off number. No invented share of stores.

outline.h2: How does the audit test site search and navigation?
outline.answerHint: The audit runs the same five query types on every store: a misspelling, a synonym, a product attribute, a SKU or model number and a non-product question such as 'returns'. Each one passes only if the first results or a helpful zero-result page answer it.
points: Visual 3: search query test sheet (see visuals). Then the checks in open text: autocomplete with product suggestions, typo tolerance, synonyms, zero-result queries that offer categories or popular products, search results that keep the filters.
Navigation checks: category labels in shopper language, a parent category that is clickable, breadcrumbs on PLP and PDP, the search field visible on mobile without opening the menu.

Keep it to the audit view. Site search design (ranking rules, merchandising) belongs to the e-commerce industry page; do not repeat its FAQ 'Does commerce design work include site search?'. No link needed here (link budget).

Cite Baymard's public figure only if the fact-checker confirms the page: '78% of shoppers use search often or every time' is in Baymard's audit guide but drawn from a premium dataset; prefer to leave it out unless a public Baymard page states it.

outline.h2: Which product listing and product page checks find the biggest leaks?
outline.answerHint: On the product listing page (PLP), check filters against the attributes shoppers compare and the product card content. On the product detail page (PDP), check the variant selector, the total delivered price and date, the size guide and the returns line next to the add-to-cart button.
points: Two short lists (ul), one for the PLP (filters per category, applied filters visible and removable, sort order, product cards with price, rating and variant swatches, load more vs pagination keeps the scroll position) and one for the PDP (images at the zoom shoppers need, variant selector that shows out-of-stock sizes, error message if no size is chosen, delivery date and shipping cost near add to cart, size guide, return policy, review display).

Reviews: the FTC Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials (16 CFR Part 465) bans fake and suppressed reviews. One sentence and a deep link to the industry page section on payment, accessibility and review rules; do not restate the rule list.
Example in hub wording: a delivery date next to the add-to-cart button. Tie return reasons (from the data pull) to the PDP checks.
This section has no image (variety and image budget): the two lists are the content.

outline.h2: What are the 12 cart and checkout checks in an e-commerce UX audit?
outline.answerHint: The 12 checks cover cost, account, form and trust: total cost shown before the payment step, guest checkout, address autocomplete, shipping address reused as billing address, inline error messages, an order summary at every step and the payment methods shoppers expect.
points: Visual 4: checkout pass/fail card with exactly 12 checks. List them once in the text version under the image. Suggested 12: (1) shipping cost and taxes visible before checkout, (2) cart editable without leaving (quantity, remove, variant), (3) guest checkout as the default, account offered after the order, (4) number of form fields counted per step, (5) address autocomplete, (6) billing address defaults to the shipping address, (7) correct mobile keyboards (numeric for card and phone), (8) inline errors that say how to fix the field, (9) entered data kept after an error, (10) order summary visible at every step, (11) payment methods shown before the payment step (cards plus wallets the audience uses), (12) promo code field that does not pull shoppers out to search for codes.

Data: Baymard's US survey of checkout abandonment reasons (extra costs too high 40%, site wanted me to create an account 18%, too long or complicated checkout 17%, did not trust the site with card details 19%). Fact-checker: confirm each figure and the year on baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate (page updated 22 September 2025). Do not cite home.ts's '$260B' figure here.
Payment page scripts: PCI DSS v4.0 requirement 6.4.3 is already on the industry page; link there in the PDP section instead and do not explain PCI here (see notes).
Explain why this is not the whole audit: a checkout UX audit alone misses shoppers who leave at search or the PDP (secondary keyword carrier).

outline.h2: How does an e-commerce UX audit cover mobile, speed and accessibility?
outline.answerHint: Mobile gets its own pass with its own GA4 numbers, speed is judged by Core Web Vitals field data (good: LCP 2.5 s or less, INP 200 ms or less, CLS 0.1 or less at the 75th percentile), and every audited template is checked against WCAG 2.2 level AA.
points: Mobile: device split from GA4 (mobile vs desktop conversion rate), thumb reach for add to cart, sticky add-to-cart bar not covering content, mobile keyboard types. Hub 'when to hire' item: mobile conversion below desktop.

Speed: cite web.dev for the thresholds and the 75th percentile. Tie INP to store interactions: tapping a filter, a colour swatch or add to cart. Use PageSpeed Insights field data (Chrome UX Report), not a single lab run.

Accessibility: Visual 5, WCAG 2.2 checkout criteria table (see visuals): 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (A), 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) (AA), 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) (AA), 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) (AA, 24 x 24 CSS px), plus 1.4.3 contrast 4.5:1 for body text (hub wording). Fact-checker: confirm numbers and levels on w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/new-in-22/.

Legal context in 2 sentences, no legal advice: many US website accessibility lawsuits are brought under ADA Title III, and there is no DOJ technical standard for private business websites, so WCAG 2.2 AA is the working benchmark (fact-checker: confirm wording; the industry page's 'US courts apply the ADA to online stores' is broader than the case law, do not repeat it). The European Accessibility Act applies to e-commerce services offered to EU consumers from 28 June 2025.
Say that the audit checks templates, not every page; a full-site accessibility audit is quoted separately (ux-audit hub FAQ wording). No overlay widgets (industry page wording).

outline.h2: How do you score and rank e-commerce UX audit findings?
outline.answerHint: Give each finding a severity rating from 1 to 4, multiply by the share of sessions that reach that page, and divide by the effort estimate in development days. Fixes with high severity, high reach and low effort go first.
points: First-hand method in site wording: every issue gets a screenshot, a severity rating from 1 to 4, a recommended fix and an effort estimate (ux-audit hub). Reach comes from the GA4 funnel exploration (affected sessions). Two senior designers score independently and then merge (ux-audit hub process); follow the hub's '2 designers', not home.ts's '1–2 designers' (see notes).

Visual 6: priority 2x2 (impact = severity x reach vs effort). Quadrant names must be our own: 'fix this sprint', 'plan the project', 'batch with the next release', 'park'. Do not use Baymard's labels.

One worked example labelled illustrative, using invented inputs that are clearly hypothetical: e.g. a severity 3 shipping-cost surprise on the cart page that every buyer sees vs a severity 4 bug in a rarely used gift-wrap option. No dollar uplift, no conversion-lift percentage.
Turn the top of the list into A/B testing hypotheses: the hub's 'A/B testing backlog' benefit; do not re-explain CRO vs UX design (hub FAQ).
Lead moment 2: a ranked list with effort in days is the deliverable stores pay for.

outline.h2: What does a self-audit of your own store miss?
outline.answerHint: A self-audit misses what your team no longer notices: you know where every menu item is, you test logged in with saved addresses, on office Wi-Fi and a desktop screen. Run the checklist yourselves first, then bring in independent evaluators when the findings will decide a redesign budget.
points: Short reasoned bullets (blind spot + why): familiarity with category names; logged-in sessions that skip guest checkout; fast devices and networks that hide INP and LCP problems; internal search terms that match the catalogue; no severity calibration across reviewers.

When an expert audit pays: use the hub 'when should an online store hire' triggers (cart abandonment rises at steady traffic and prices, mobile conversion below desktop, replatforming project starts, sizing questions and returns rise) and deep-link that hub section instead of listing all five.
Do NOT rebuild the provider matrix from ux-audit-agency-vs-freelancer (freelancer vs agency vs AI tool vs in-house). No AI-tool section. Do not link that post (another silo).

If audit then redesign: the hub vs table says stores without funnel evidence start with the UX audit, then redesign the weakest templates. One sentence, deep link to /services/ecommerce-ux-design-services/#e-commerce-ux-design-vs-ux-audit.

outline.h2: What should you send to get an e-commerce UX audit quote?
outline.answerHint: Send the store URL and platform, the templates and devices in scope, GA4 read access or a funnel export, your top site search queries and any accessibility deadline. With those, an audit can be scoped at a fixed price.
points: Short ul of 6 scope inputs, store-specific: store platform (Shopify, BigCommerce, Adobe Commerce, custom), templates in scope (home, PLP, PDP, cart, checkout, account), devices, markets and languages, GA4 view access, top 50 search queries plus zero-result list, accessibility deadline (EAA, contract). Do not reuse the 'six scope inputs' list or 'scope sheet' visual from ux-audit-agency-vs-freelancer: different items, plain list, no form graphic.

Price: one sentence with the published figures from the hub comparison table: a UX audit runs $5,000–$15,000 over 2–3 weeks; a full e-commerce UX design engagement that redesigns and tests the funnel templates runs $25,000–$60,000 over 4–8 weeks. Deep link to /services/ecommerce-ux-design-services/#e-commerce-ux-design-vs-ux-audit. Do not restate the hub's near-$25,000 / near-$60,000 example projects.
Main lead moment and offer (see leadAngle). Second UP link to the hub. Close with the next step to /contact/.

faqs.q: How often should an online store run a UX audit?
faqs.hint: Tie it to events, not a calendar: before a replatforming project, after a theme or checkout change, when the funnel exploration shows a new drop at one step, and before the peak season build freeze. No invented 'every 6 months' rule (SERP pages state it without a source).

faqs.q: Does an e-commerce UX audit include accessibility?
faqs.hint: Yes. Each audited template is checked against WCAG 2.2 level AA; a full-site accessibility audit is quoted separately (ux-audit hub FAQ wording). 2 sentences.

faqs.q: Is an e-commerce UX audit the same as a CRO audit?
faqs.hint: No. The UX audit finds and ranks usability issues with evidence; conversion rate optimization (CRO) tests single changes with A/B testing. The audit's ranked list feeds the A/B test backlog. Do not copy the hub FAQ sentence on 'e-commerce UX design vs CRO'.

faqs.q: Can a Shopify UX audit recommend changes to the checkout?
faqs.hint: Yes, within the platform's limits. Fact-checker must confirm current Shopify checkout customisation (Checkout Extensibility / checkout UI extensions; checkout.liquid deprecated for Plus stores). Each finding should say whether it is a theme change, an app change or a checkout setting. Keep it to 2–3 sentences; no promise about what Shopify allows beyond the confirmed facts.

faqs.q: Should you audit the old store before replatforming?
faqs.hint: Yes. An audit before the move lists the issues to fix in the new templates instead of copying them across. The hub names a replatforming project, e.g. a custom store moving to Shopify, as a trigger. 2 sentences.

leadAngle: Three moments. (1) End of the data-pull section: many stores find their GA4 e-commerce events missing or duplicated; we check tracking in the first days of the audit before trusting any drop-off number. (2) End of the scoring section: a ranked list with severity, reach and effort in development days is what an expert audit hands over, and what a team scoring its own store struggles to calibrate. (3) Main offer in 'What should you send to get an e-commerce UX audit quote?': send the store URL, platform, templates and devices in scope, GA4 access and the top search queries, and get a fixed-scope e-commerce UX audit proposal within the published $5,000–$15,000 range for 2–3 weeks (link the hub comparison table), with the option to continue into the 4–8 week e-commerce UX design engagement for the weakest templates. A first step the site already offers (home.ts ctaBand): a 45-minute UX audit session in which we review the product and identify the top three friction points; do not call it free (home.ts does not). The writer adds one specific invitation, e.g. 'send us your funnel exploration and we will tell you which step to audit first'.
